transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a lot of things, really, but what finally made me pick up the phone and make this appointment—which, honestly, I've been putting off for months, maybe even a year, if I'm being completely honest with myself—is the physical toll it's taking. I mean, my neck, my shoulders, my jaw... they are just constantly, incredibly tight. Almost all the time now. It's like... you know that feeling when you're waiting for the other shoe to drop? Like you're physically bracing yourself for some terrible news? That's how my body feels. And it's not just when I'm at school dealing with the kids or grading papers—I teach high school, so there's always something going on there—but it's even when I'm just sitting at my desk during a free period, or when I'm finally home, sitting on the couch, trying to just watch TV and unwind at night. My wife keeps telling me I look like a coiled spring, and she's not wrong. I catch myself clenching my jaw so hard I get these headaches, and my shoulders are practically up by my ears half the day. I try to roll them out, do some stretches, but the tension just comes right back. It's exhausting, it really is, just carrying all this tightness around every single day.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge?

Anxious or on edge? Oh, absolutely. I mean, "on edge" is probably the most accurate way you could possibly put it. I just feel so incredibly wound up for most of the day. It's this underlying... I don't know, this constant hum of just waiting for something else to go wrong. 

And it really shows up in my behavior, too, which I'm starting to notice more and more. Like, when I'm in the classroom—and I've been teaching a long time, I know this curriculum inside and out, so I shouldn't be nervous in front of a bunch of teenagers—but I catch myself just pacing endlessly. Up and down the rows, back and forth by the whiteboard, just constantly moving. I can't seem to just stand still at the podium anymore. 

And then, the second the bell rings and it's my prep period or I have a five-minute break between classes, instead of sitting down to grade or just, you know, taking a deep breath, I'm immediately pulling out my phone. We're having some work done on the house right now, and I am just obsessively checking for messages from the contractor. I'll check it, put it in my pocket, and two minutes later I'm pulling it right back out, just absolutely convinced he's going to text me that they found black mold or the foundation is cracked or some other massive problem. It's just this nonstop feeling that the next disaster is right around the corner, so my brain and my body are just constantly running at top speed, waiting for it.
Do you find yourself having repetitive thoughts that you can't seem to get out of your head?

Repetitive thoughts? Yes. Oh, yes, absolutely. It's like... it's like a broken record, or maybe more like a snowball rolling down a hill, just getting bigger and bigger and I can't do anything to stop it. I try, you know? I really do try. I'll be standing there in the middle of a lesson—say we're doing the French Revolution, which I've taught a hundred times, I know exactly where the lecture is going—and I can tell myself, "Okay, stop thinking about the house, stop thinking about the bills, just focus on the class in front of you." 

But then, it's just... one small thought creeps in. Maybe I remember an invoice from the plumber that I haven't paid yet, or I look out at the desks and see a student who's been falling behind, and suddenly, it's off to the races. That one little thought sets off this whole chain reaction of what-ifs that I just cannot shut down. If it's the invoice, I start thinking, "What if I forgot to pay it? What if they put a lien on the house? What if we lose the house?" If it's the student, it's, "What if they fail? What if their parents complain to the principal? What if I get put on probation? What if I lose my job at 55 and can't find another one?" 

It just spirals, and it plays on a loop. I can physically feel my chest tightening while I'm trying to explain the Reign of Terror, because my brain is running through ten different catastrophic scenarios about my own life. I try to shake my head, literally shake it to clear the thoughts, but they just circle back around. It's exhausting, doctor, it really is, just having my own mind constantly hijacking my attention like that. I can't seem to just have a thought and let it go. It always has to turn into this massive, uncontrollable worry.
Are you finding it harder to teach or perform your job duties because of these worries and physical symptoms?

Well, yes, actually. It's... it's definitely bleeding into my work, which is incredibly frustrating because, like I said, I've been doing this for a long time. I pride myself on being prepared, you know? I usually have my lesson plans mapped out weeks in advance, and I'm the guy who gets papers graded and handed back by the next day. But lately? Lately, it's just... I can't seem to focus long enough to get it all done. The lesson prep is falling by the wayside because I'll sit down at my desk with my planner, and instead of writing out the curriculum for next week, I'm just staring at the wall, completely consumed by those spiraling thoughts about the house or the bills. 

And the grading... oh, the grading has just piled up. I have a stack of essays on my desk right now that have been sitting there for almost two weeks. Two weeks! That's completely unlike me. I look at them, and my jaw gets tight, and my shoulders go up, and I just feel so overwhelmed by the sheer volume of it all, combined with everything else running through my head, that I just push them aside. 

It's gotten so bad that I actually had to step back from some of my extracurriculars, too. I usually help manage the community theater productions in town—building sets, coordinating the stage crew, that sort of thing. It's something I've always loved, a real passion project for me. We were gearing up for the spring musical, and I just... I had to tell them I couldn't do it. I couldn't handle the scheduling and the late nights on top of teaching, not with my brain constantly spinning like a top. I felt terrible letting them down, I really did, but I just couldn't keep up with all of it anymore. The balls were starting to drop, and I had to let something go before I completely fell apart at school.
Are you experiencing difficulties in your relationships with family or friends due to your worries and physical symptoms?

Relationships with family or friends? Um... no, not really. I mean, I guess I haven't really noticed any major issues there. It's funny you ask that, though, because you'd think with how wound up I am all the time, I'd be snapping at everyone, right? But honestly, my wife has been an absolute saint through all this house renovation stuff. She just kind of lets me pace around and check my phone, and she doesn't make a big deal out of it. 

And as for friends, well, I don't see them as much right now anyway, what with stepping back from the theater and all. When I do see folks, like the other teachers in the breakroom, I think I do a pretty good job of keeping it together. I mean, I'm sure they notice I'm a little distracted, but nobody's said anything, and I haven't had any arguments or falling outs or anything like that. I just sort of keep my head down and try to get through the day. So, no, I wouldn't say my relationships are suffering... it's more just me, internally, dealing with all this constant noise.
Are there any activities or situations that you used to enjoy but now avoid because of your worries or physical symptoms?

Avoid? Hmm. Well, like I said, I stepped back from the community theater, but I wouldn't say I'm *avoiding* it because of the worries, exactly. It was more of a time management thing, just trying to keep my head above water with school. As for other things... I don't think so. I mean, I still go to the grocery store, I still go to work, obviously, even though it's harder right now. 

I still go out to dinner with my wife on Friday nights. We have this little Italian place we've been going to for years, Luigi's, over on 4th Street. Best garlic knots in town, hands down. I'll admit, sometimes I'm sitting there at the table and my mind is racing about the house foundation or whether I remembered to submit the attendance report, and I might not be the most attentive dinner companion, but I still go. I don't stay home just to worry, if that makes sense. 

I still try to watch the football games on Sunday, too. Usually, I'd have a couple of the guys over, maybe grill some burgers, but lately I've just been watching them by myself. Not because I'm avoiding the guys, but just because the thought of hosting, of cleaning the house and making sure there's enough food and drinks, it just feels like one more massive task on a to-do list that I'm already failing at. But I still watch the games. So, no, I don't think I'm actively avoiding any specific situations or activities. I'm just... doing them while being completely consumed by this constant loop of anxiety. It's like I'm present physically, but mentally, I'm a million miles away, trying to put out fires that haven't even started yet. But I haven't stopped doing the things I usually do.
Do you ever have episodes where you feel an intense fear or discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes and includes symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or shortness of breath?

Intense fear... like a peak? You mean like a panic attack or something? No, no, I don't think I've ever had anything quite like that. It's funny you mention the racing heart and sweating, though, because I do get those things, but it's not like... it's not like a sudden explosion, you know? It's more of a slow burn. 

Like, I'll be sitting in the staff room, just trying to eat a sandwich, and I'll start thinking about the contractor for the house, and whether he's actually going to show up on Tuesday like he promised, because last time he said Tuesday and he didn't come until Thursday, and that threw off the plumber, and then the whole schedule was a mess. And as I'm thinking about this, I can feel my heart rate creeping up, just a little bit faster, a little bit faster, and my palms might get a little clammy. And the tension in my neck starts—right back here at the base of my skull, it just tightens up like a vise. But it doesn't happen in minutes. It's not a sudden spike. It just sort of builds and builds over the course of the day until I'm just this tightly wound ball of nerves by the time the final bell rings. 

And the shortness of breath... I don't know if I'd call it shortness of breath, exactly. It's more like I forget to breathe deeply? Like I'm taking these shallow little breaths because my chest feels so tight from all the worrying. My wife actually pointed it out the other day. We were watching TV, just some home improvement show—which, in hindsight, was probably a terrible choice given our current situation—and she looked over at me and said, "Honey, take a breath." And I realized I had been sort of holding my breath, or just breathing really shallowly, because my mind was a million miles away, calculating the cost of drywall. 

So, I definitely get the physical stuff—the tight muscles, the stomach aches, the heart beating a bit faster—but it's a constant, low-level hum of anxiety. It never really peaks and then goes away. It just stays with me, all day, every day. It's exhausting, honestly, but it's not that sudden, intense rush of fear you're describing. It's just a continuous, grinding worry that never really lets up.
Do you experience any gastrointestinal problems like stomachaches or irritable bowel syndrome?

Stomachaches? Irritable bowel syndrome? Well, um, no, not irritable bowel syndrome or anything like that. I mean, my stomach isn't exactly made of cast iron these days, but I wouldn't call it a major problem. 

I did mention the stomach aches earlier, didn't I? Yeah, I get those. But it's not like... it's not like I'm running to the bathroom all day or doubled over in pain. It's more of a... a churning, I guess you could say. Like this constant, uneasy feeling right in the pit of my stomach. It’s funny, my grandmother used to call it having "butterflies," but this isn't butterflies. Butterflies make you think of being nervous before a big date or, you know, stepping out on stage for opening night at the community theater. This is more like... like having a rock sitting in there. A heavy, dull ache that just kind of lingers. 

It usually hits me worst in the mornings, right before I have to leave for school. I’ll be standing in the kitchen, pouring my coffee—which I probably shouldn't be drinking so much of, but how else am I supposed to get through first period history?—and I'll just feel this knot tightening up in my gut. And then I start thinking about the lesson plan, and whether the kids are actually going to pay attention to the unit on the Industrial Revolution, or if they're just going to be staring at their phones under the desks again. And then, of course, my mind jumps right back to the house, and whether the electrician pulled the right permits for the rewiring we're doing in the kitchen. 

So, yeah, my stomach definitely acts up, but it's completely tied to the worrying. It's not like a medical... well, I mean, I guess it is medical, but it's not like I have a stomach bug or food poisoning or IBS. It's just my body reacting to this endless loop of stress. I haven't changed my diet or anything, although I probably eat a little less than I used to because I just don't have the appetite when my stomach feels like it's tied in knots. My wife made this incredible roast chicken on Sunday—she really is a fantastic cook, uses this rosemary and lemon rub that's just out of this world—and I barely touched it. I just pushed it around my plate because my stomach was just churning about the upcoming week. So, no IBS, but definitely a lot of that heavy, nervous stomach ache feeling.
Are there any places or situations that you're avoiding because you're worried something might go wrong?

Avoiding places because something might go wrong... hmm. No, no, I really don't think so. It kind of goes back to what I was saying a few minutes ago about not really avoiding things in general. I don't have this fear that, you know, if I go to the hardware store, the roof is going to cave in, or if I drive on the interstate, I'm guaranteed to get into a terrible accident. It's not that kind of... catastrophic worry about the location itself. 

My worries are more tied to my responsibilities, I guess you could say, even though they feel completely overwhelming. Like, take the grocery store. I go to the grocery store down on Elm Street every Sunday morning to get our staples for the week. Have for years. I certainly don't avoid it. But while I'm pushing the cart down the cereal aisle, I'm not worried about slipping on a wet floor or having some kind of public emergency. Instead, I'm just standing there staring at the boxes of oats, completely paralyzed because I'm thinking about whether the contractor ordered the right grade of lumber for the subfloor, and if he didn't, is the whole addition going to fail inspection, and if it fails inspection, are we going to have to pay another massive fee that we haven't budgeted for... and suddenly I realize I've been standing in front of the cereal for ten minutes and someone is clearing their throat behind me trying to get by. 

But I still went to the store, you see? I don't stay home. And school, it's the exact same thing. I don't avoid the classroom or the teachers' lounge. I'm there every single day, pulling into the parking lot at 7:15 AM sharp. I might be sitting at my desk feeling like my stomach is tied in a knot, like I mentioned earlier, worrying about whether my students are actually retaining anything or if the administration is going to spring a surprise observation on me when I'm behind on grading, but I don't avoid the building. I've never called in sick just because I was afraid a specific disaster would happen at the school. 

So, no, I'm not avoiding any places or situations. The anxiety just... it just comes with me wherever I go. It's like this incredibly heavy backpack I can't take off, whether I'm at the supermarket, at school, or sitting in my own living room trying to watch television. It doesn't stop me from walking through the front doors of a place. I just carry all that dread inside with me once I'm there.
Is your worrying focused on just a few specific things, like the house renovation and work, or does it seem to spread out and cover almost everything you think about?

Spread out? Oh, it definitely spreads out. It's not just the house and school, though those are certainly the loudest ones on the radar. It’s more like... like a chain reaction, I guess? One thought just triggers the next, and before I know it, I'm miles away from where I started. 

I'll be sitting in my armchair after dinner, right? Just trying to read a biography, trying to unwind. But my mind keeps jumping from the renovation—like, whether the contractors missed something crucial in the subfloor that's going to cause the whole addition to settle unevenly in a few years—and then, almost instantly, it pivots to work. I'll start worrying about whether my lesson plans are slipping, if I'm not engaging the sophomores enough, because they just seemed so checked out during my lecture on the New Deal yesterday. 

And from there, it's a straight line right to the extracurriculars. I advise the robotics club, you see, and I'll just start agonizing over whether the robotics kids are behind on their build schedule for the spring competition. We only have a few weeks left, and the autonomous programming is a mess, and if they fail at the regional meet, that's on me. I'm the advisor, I should be managing their time better. 

And then... well, then it just sort of balloons into this overarching dread about my personal life. I start thinking about whether I'm disappointing my wife and my family by not keeping everything under control. She's been so patient with me being distracted all the time, but I can't shake this heavy feeling that I'm letting everyone down because my brain is just so scattered. It’s like I can’t just compartmentalize anymore. The worry just spills over the edges of whatever I'm doing and covers absolutely everything I think about. I could be doing something completely mindless, like mowing the front lawn, and I'll end up stressing about whether I remembered to renew the car registration or if I accidentally offended the principal at the last staff meeting. It just... it never stays in one box, you know? It just goes everywhere.
Is there one particular area of your life where you feel your worrying is most prominent?

Well, gosh, like I was just saying a moment ago, it’s incredibly difficult to isolate just one particular area because of how they all connect. It’s like asking which part of a spiderweb is the most important, you know? If I pull on one string, the whole thing shakes. So, no, I wouldn't say there's one single prominent area, because my mind just keeps jumping constantly between all of them. 

It's exactly like that chain reaction I was describing—one minute I'm completely fixated on the renovation and whether the contractors missed something structural in the house, something that's going to cost us thousands to fix down the line. And then, without even taking a breath, my brain just pivots to school, and I'm stressing over whether my lesson plans are slipping and if I'm shortchanging my students. Teaching isn't just reading dates from a textbook, you have to bring it alive, and when I'm distracted, I know I'm not doing that. 

And then, of course, it's right on to the extracurriculars, worrying about whether the robotics kids are behind on their build, which, as their advisor, falls entirely on my shoulders. We really only have a few weeks until the regional competition, and their autonomous code is just a mess, and I feel completely responsible for that. 

And then, ultimately, it all circles back to this profound, heavy fear that I'm disappointing my wife and my family by not keeping everything under control. She's so supportive, but I know it must be exhausting to live with someone who is always a million miles away in his own head. So, the prominence isn't in the house or the school or the family—it's the jumping itself. It's the fact that my brain refuses to just pick one thing to worry about, so it just bounces from the house to the lessons to the club to my marriage, all at once, on this endless loop.
Are you finding that your worrying is significantly interfering with your ability to enjoy time with friends and family or perform daily tasks?

Interfering... yes. Yes, I'm afraid it really is, and that's probably the most frustrating part of all this, to be perfectly honest with you. It's one thing to feel terrible inside your own head, but it's another entirely when it starts spilling over into the things you actually need to get done, the things people rely on you for. 

Take my job, for instance. I've always prided myself on being incredibly organized—you really have to be, when you're teaching high schoolers, or they'll eat you alive. But lately, I just... I'll sit down at my desk with a stack of essays, say, the sophomores' papers on the Great Depression, and I just stare at them. My mind starts spinning with all those other worries I mentioned, the house, the robotics club, the family, and before I know it, an hour has gone by and I haven't graded a single paper. So, I've really started falling behind on my lesson prep and my grading. It just piles up on my desk, and my lesson plans are getting thrown together at the last minute, which makes me feel even worse because I know I'm not giving the kids my best effort.

And it's not just work, either. It's bleeding into the things I do for fun, or at least the things I *used* to do for fun. Outside of school, I've always been very involved in our local community theater. I usually manage a good portion of the backstage operations—coordinating the volunteers, making sure the props are organized, helping sort out the schedules, that sort of thing. It's something I've loved doing for years, a real creative outlet for me and a great way to see friends. But this season... I just had to step back. I actually gave up parts of the community-theater work I usually manage because I simply couldn't keep up with all of it anymore. 

The mental bandwidth just isn't there. I'd be at the theater trying to organize a rehearsal schedule, and my brain would be agonizing over the grading I was behind on, or the subfloor at the house, and I just felt like I was dropping the ball everywhere. I was forgetting things, getting overwhelmed by simple logistical questions from the director... so I had to tell them I couldn't do it this time around. Which really broke my heart, honestly. I hate letting people down, but it just feels like everything is slipping through my fingers because I can't focus on what's right in front of me.
Do you feel like your worrying is causing you a lot of distress?

Distress... gosh, I'm really not sure if I'd use that specific word. What exactly do you mean by distress, Doctor? Because, you know, as a teacher, words matter a great deal to me, and when I hear "distress," my mind immediately goes to, oh, I don't know, a ship sinking at sea, or someone having a complete and utter breakdown, sobbing in the middle of the grocery aisle. And that’s not really what’s happening to me. I haven't noticed anything quite that dramatic. I'm still getting up at 5:30 every morning, I'm still brewing the coffee—my wife and I always have a dark French roast first thing—and I'm still driving to the high school and standing in front of my students. So if distress means completely falling apart at the seams and not being able to function at a basic level, then I don't have that to give you. 

But... well, I just don't know. If you mean, am I just thoroughly fed up with it all? Then sure. It’s incredibly frustrating. Like yesterday afternoon, I tried to just sit on the front porch for ten minutes, just to watch the neighborhood go by and maybe catch my breath before dinner. And instead of just enjoying the quiet, I’m sitting there pinching the bridge of my nose, completely wrapped up in whether the robotics team is going to blow their budget on sensors they don't actually need, and whether that contractor is going to overcharge us for the drywall work on the addition. It’s just this constant, heavy annoyance. It’s tiring, certainly. 

But distress? I honestly couldn't say for sure. It just feels like my brain is a radio left on scan, constantly jumping from station to station, and I can't seem to find the power button to just turn the darn thing off for five minutes. Does that count as distress in your field? Because to me, it's just... well, it's just my life right now, and I'm not really sure how to categorize it beyond just being utterly sick and tired of the noise.
Are you finding it difficult to fulfill your responsibilities at home or maintain your relationships with others because of your worrying?

Well, I know I touched on this a bit earlier when we were talking about my daily tasks, but... yes. It really is. Because, you see, it’s all connected. Like I said before, I've started falling behind on my lesson prep and my grading, and when that happens, I don't just leave it at the high school. I pack all those papers up in my leather briefcase—the one my wife got me for our twentieth anniversary, actually—and I bring it all home. 

And then it just sits there on the kitchen island. Just staring at me. So instead of, you know, being present with my wife, helping chop vegetables for dinner, or actually sitting down to have a meaningful conversation with her about how her day went, I'm just pacing around the kitchen, completely consumed by the fact that I'm behind on everything. So my responsibilities at home, even just the basic responsibility of being a supportive partner, are definitely taking a huge hit because I'm just not mentally in the room. I'm a ghost in my own house.

And as for relationships... well, it's the exact same story with the theater situation I mentioned a few minutes ago. I know I told you how I had to give up parts of the community-theater work I usually manage because I just couldn't keep up with all of it anymore, but what I didn't really get into was how much that actually isolates me. Those people at the theater—the director, the lighting folks, the volunteers—they're some of my closest friends in town. We used to go out to the diner for pie and coffee after late rehearsals. It was our ritual. 

Now? I barely see any of them. Since I had to back out of managing things, I feel entirely too guilty to even text them, because I feel like I left them in the lurch right before the spring musical. I worry they resent me for it, or that they think I just don't care about the production, which couldn't be further from the truth. So, yes, the friendships are absolutely fading, and my wife is stuck living with a man who can't even focus enough to ask her how she's doing. It’s just... it feels like every connection I have is slowly fraying because I can't get my head on straight.
Are you feeling like your worrying is significantly impacting your ability to function in your daily life or maintain your relationships?

Well, I know I've been talking your ear off about all this, and I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit, but yes, it really is. It's just... it's like a domino effect, you know? I mentioned the schoolwork earlier, how I've started falling behind on lesson prep and grading. And that's not a small thing for me. I mean, I teach history, and if you aren't prepared with a solid narrative, the kids just tune you out completely. But I'll sit there with my red pen, looking at a stack of papers on the Industrial Revolution, and my mind is just a million miles away, worrying about the house or the robotics club or whatever else has decided to take up residence in my brain that day. So the papers don't get graded, the lessons aren't prepped, and I end up feeling like a complete fraud standing in front of my classroom.

And it's the exact same story with my personal life, which I know I also touched on. The theater... God, that really hurts. I've always been the guy who keeps things running backstage, making sure the props are where they need to be, the cast knows their call times, all those little logistical things that make a show actually happen. But I just had to step away. I gave up parts of the community-theater work I usually manage because I just couldn't keep up with all of it anymore. The mental energy it takes to organize all those moving parts... I just don't have it right now. And because I stepped back, I'm not seeing those friends, I'm not part of that community the way I used to be, and I feel terrible about it. I feel like I've let them down, and I worry they're upset with me, which just adds another layer to the whole mess. So, yes, to answer your question, it's absolutely impacting my daily life and my relationships. It feels like I'm just dropping balls left and right, and I don't know how to stop it.
Do you feel like your worrying is causing you significant emotional pain or discomfort?

Emotional pain... you know, we seem to be circling back to the vocabulary of it all, just like when you asked about distress earlier. Words are just... well, they're important to get right, especially in a setting like this. "Pain" is a very strong word. When I hear "emotional pain," my mind immediately goes to true grief. Like when my father passed away back in '08. Now, that was a deep, heavy ache, the kind where you feel it right behind your ribs and it almost physically hurts to just get out of bed in the morning. I am certainly not experiencing anything like that. 

And discomfort... well, I suppose that's a milder term, but even then, it makes me think of, oh, sitting in a chair with a bad spring, or wearing a scratchy wool sweater without an undershirt. I guess you could say my mind feels a bit scratchy, but I wouldn't say I'm in actual pain or even significant discomfort in that emotional sense. It’s really just that relentless mental exhaustion I was telling you about before. 

I mean, I'm not crying myself to sleep, I'm not feeling this profound emotional agony... it's just the gears constantly turning, grinding away at the lesson plans or the drywall contractor or the theater group. I suppose you could argue that being entirely unable to shut my brain off is uncomfortable, sure, but... significant emotional pain? No, no, I really don't think I'd classify it as that. I don't mean to be difficult or split hairs with you, Doctor, it's just... as an educator, I want to be precise. I want to make sure I'm giving you the most accurate picture of my day-to-day, and "pain" just doesn't seem to fit what's happening up here. It's just noisy. Very, very noisy.
Do you feel like your worrying is causing you a lot of emotional distress?

Distress. Yes, see, I think that is a much better word for it than pain. Distress... yes, absolutely. Because distress implies a sort of, well, a state of being overwhelmed and troubled, doesn't it? And that is exactly what it is. It’s deeply distressing to watch yourself fail at the things you’ve always been so capable of handling. 

I know I’m sounding like an absolute broken record today, and I do apologize for circling back to the exact same examples yet again, but it really all just comes back to the teaching and the theater. That's where this distress truly manifests for me. To be sitting at my kitchen island, knowing I am actively falling behind on my lesson prep and my grading... for a man who prides himself on being a thorough, dedicated educator, that is incredibly distressing. I’ll look at a stack of essays on the Gilded Age, and instead of just diving in with my red pen like I've done for nearly thirty years, I just feel this heavy, sinking panic because I know I'm not doing my job properly. 

And then, of course, there's the theater situation. Having to actually give up the parts of the community-theater work I usually manage... I had to walk away from it, as I mentioned, because I simply couldn't keep up with all the moving parts anymore. My brain just wouldn't hold it all. And the distress of that—of having to admit defeat, of looking at the director and saying 'I can't do this,' of knowing I'm letting down a production I care about... yes, that causes me a great deal of distress. It's the realization that I am shrinking my own life down because I can't manage the worry. So, if we're using that specific word, then yes, I would absolutely say it's causing me a very significant amount of it.
Are you finding that your worrying is interfering with your ability to perform your job as a teacher or maintain your relationships with your family and friends?

Well, Doctor, I feel a bit like we’re caught in a loop here. I know I can be quite talkative—my late wife used to say I could filibuster a brick wall—but I do believe I’ve been saying exactly that for the last few minutes. I don't mean to sound frustrated, I know you have a specific list of questions you need to get through for your assessment, but yes, it is absolutely interfering. 

To put it as plainly as I can, since we seem to be revisiting the point: professionally, as I detailed just a moment ago, I've started falling behind on lesson prep and grading. It isn't just a minor slip-up or a case of the Sunday scaries. It’s a fundamental inability to sit down at my desk, focus on the material, and do the job I’ve done successfully for nearly thirty years. I stare at the students' essays, and the worry just completely overrides my ability to process the words on the page. I can't build a cohesive lesson plan when my mind is darting in a hundred different directions.
